mythology.body:
The ​stories of ‌Sarnath ‌place ​first sermon, ​deer ​park at ​the ​center ‌of a ​living ​mythological world.

### ‌Origins ​(Myth)

Sarnath ‌appears ​in ‌buddhist tradition ​as ​first sermon, ​deer ​park. ​The name's ‌meaning, ​"Lord of ‌the ​deer", ‌shapes the ​narratives ‌told about ​this ‌figure.

### ​Worship and ​Memory ‌(Cult)

Devotees ‌and ‌later tradition-keepers ​preserved ​Sarnath ‌in ritual, ​text, ​and iconography, ‌ensuring ​the ​name survived ‌into ​the modern ‌scholarly ​record.

​The myths ​of ​Sarnath survive ‌in ‌fragments, ​summaries, and ‌later ​retellings. Each ​version ‌reflects the ‌interests ‌of ‌its tellers ​— ‌poets, priests, ​philosophers, ​and ​scholars. The ‌PuniCodex ​entry does ​not ​privilege ‌a single ​version; ​it gathers ​the ‌attestations ​so that ‌readers ​can compare ‌them. ​The restoration ‌Sarnath ‌gives ​the figure ​a ​stable name ​around ‌which ‌these variants ​orbit.

​Were ‌such ​evidence ​to ​surface, ​it ‌would take ‌recognizable ​forms: ‌votive ​or ​dedicatory ‌inscriptions ‌naming सर्नथ्, ‌sanctuary ‌or ​cult ‌remains ​tied ​to first ​sermon ‌and ​iconography ​matching ​its ‌traditional ​attributes (name ​and ​domain). ‌Each ​candidate ‌would ​be ‌weighed against ​the ‌reconstructed ‌form ​of ​the ​name ​before entering ‌the ‌scholarly ​record.

overview.body:
**Sarnath** ​(*sarnath*) — ‌First ‌Sermon, Deer ​Park · ​Lord ​of the ​deer ​— belongs ‌to ​the Buddhist ​tradition, where ‌it ​is catalogued ‌under ​the domain ‌"First ​Sermon, Deer ​Park". The ​name ​means "Lord ​of ‌the deer"[^1].

​**Sarnath** ‌is the ​deer ‌park outside ​ancient Benares ‌where, ​weeks after ‌his ​awakening at ​Bodh ‌Gayā, the ‌Buddha delivered ‌the ​**first sermon** ​and ‌set the ​**Wheel ​of Dhamma** ‌turning. Sacred ​to ​the Buddhist ‌tradition, ​it marks ‌the ​founding moment ​of the ​teaching ​and of ‌the ‌Sangha itself.[^2]

​PuniCodex ‌records the ​canonical scholarly ​spelling ‌**Sarnath** and ‌serves ‌its temple ‌at ​[its temple](https://punicodex.com/sarnath/). ‌The displayed ​form ​is ASCII-equivalent ​— ‌a description ​computed ​from the ​displayed ‌form itself. ​The plain ​ASCII ​form *sarnath* ‌contains ​the same ‌letters: ​no recovered ‌diacritics or ​special ‌encoding is ‌claimed. ​The work ​here ​is consistent ​citation, capitalization, ‌provenance, ‌and cultural ​context[^3].

the-name.body:
The ​name ‌is attested ‌in ​Devanagari ​as **सर्नथ्**. ​Etymologically ​it ​means "Lord ‌of ​the ​deer"[^1].

The ‌canonical ​spelling ‌**Sarnath** ​matches the ‌conventional ​scholarly ​romanization. The ​plain ​ASCII ​form *sarnath* ‌contains ​the ‌same letters, ​so ‌no ​lost ‌diacritics or ​encoding ‌transition ​is claimed. ​The ‌editorial ‌work is ‌to ​fix ​one reviewed ‌reference ​spelling, ​preserve ‌capitalization and ​provenance, ​and ‌keep the ​original ‌evidence ​visible. The ​displayed ​form ​is ‌ASCII-equivalent — ‌a ​description ‌computed from ​the ​displayed ‌form itself.

meditation.body: Sarnath ​teaches a ‌distinction easy ‌to miss: ​between the ​event ​and the ​announcement. The ​enlightenment at ‌Bodh ​Gayā was ​the event ‌— solitary, ​silent, complete. ‌Sarnath ​was the ‌announcement, and ​the tradition ​insists the ​second ​was nearly ​withheld. The ‌Buddha's hesitation ​in ‌the Vinaya ​account is ‌one of ​the most ‌human ​moments in ‌scripture: a ​teacher who ​doubts ‌that anyone ‌will understand ‌him, persuaded ​finally by ​a ‌god's plea ​and by ​the few ‌beings 'with ​little ​dust in ‌their eyes.' ​The first ‌sermon ​is therefore ​not merely ​the Buddhist ​Genesis; it ‌is ‌the founding ​act of ‌communication — ​the decision ​that ‌an insight ‌kept private ‌would die, ‌while ​an insight ‌spoken aloud, ​even clumsily, ​even to ​five ‌skeptics, could ​turn the ​wheel of ​a ‌world. The ​deer-park setting ​is the ​doctrine in ‌landscape ​form: gentleness, ‌creatures unafraid ​of the ‌hunter, as ​the ‌precondition of ‌truth-telling. Every ​later sermon, ​commentary, ​and sangha ​stands in ‌the footprint ‌of that ​afternoon.[^1]
